tagline: From Petersburg to Appomattox, a driving tour follows Lee’s retreat
intro: Lee’s Retreat links Petersburg with Appomattox Court House on a driving tour of the army’s withdrawal. The National Park Service recommends the tour for following the Appomattox Campaign, with historical highway markers connecting battlefields and villages. At Sailor’s Creek, interpretive trails lead from the visitor center toward the creek and the positions where Union and Confederate troops fought. Petersburg stands at the Appomattox River’s fall line, where Piedmont bedrock meets the coastal plain.

The route’s historical thread is a struggle over movement and supplies. Union victories at Five Forks and Petersburg forced Lee to evacuate Petersburg and Richmond on the night of April 2–3, 1865. He sought supplies at Farmville, but Union forces cut off the line of retreat at Sailor’s Creek on April 6. Three days later, Lee surrendered the Army of Northern Virginia to Grant at Appomattox Court House.

For a westward journey, begin in the Petersburg area and follow the tour through Amelia Court House toward Sailor’s Creek. Continue to High Bridge, where the former railroad crossing over the Appomattox River is now part of a walking, cycling and equestrian trail. Finish at Appomattox Court House, the preserved village containing the surrender site. The visitor center occupies the rebuilt courthouse.

moments.title: Sailor's Creek Battlefield
moments.text: At Sailor’s Creek on April 6, 1865, Union forces cut off Lee’s retreat toward supplies at Farmville. They captured approximately 7,700 combatants and eight Confederate generals. The Overton-Hillsman House became a field hospital, with wounded Union and Confederate soldiers treated inside and on its lawn. A few days later, wagons carried the wounded to a larger hospital at Burkeville Junction. The restored house is furnished to show both its hospital use and its role as the Hillsman family’s home. Seven interpretive hiking trails cross the battlefield park. The Kershaw Trail leads to the creek where Union troops crossed to attack.

moments.title: High Bridge
moments.text: High Bridge began as a Southside Railroad crossing in 1854, connecting Petersburg with Lynchburg over the Appomattox River. On April 7, 1865, Confederate engineers set it on fire as Union troops approached. Three wooden spans burned; Union engineers cut away a fourth burning span to stop the destruction. Rail traffic resumed that September after repairs. The last Norfolk Southern train crossed in 2004, and the company donated the abandoned line to Virginia in 2006. Restoration of the bridge completed the trail’s opening in April 2012. Along the trail, telegraph poles and cement railroad mile markers remain.

moments.title: Appomattox Court House
moments.text: The surrender took place in a house, not the courthouse. On April 9, 1865, Lee met Grant at the McLean House and signed the terms; the Army of Northern Virginia laid down its arms on April 12. The war continued after that surrender. Before becoming the county seat, the village was called Clover Hill, a stop on the Richmond–Lynchburg stagecoach road. The village had already begun declining after the railroad bypassed it in 1854. The McLean House was later dismantled, then reconstructed and reopened in 1949. The Clover Hill Tavern survives as an original nineteenth-century building, while the visitor center occupies the rebuilt courthouse.
